qa_notes: Clear, well-structured, no OCR issues; QA2 scored 0 because the paper addresses general business-process-simulation quality assessment (loan application, call-centre, academic-credential, procure-to-pay processes), not a software-engineering-specific context.
research_question: How can the quality of a Business Process Simulation (BPS) model be measured with respect to its ability to accurately replicate observed process behavior, across multiple process perspectives (control-flow, temporal, resource, congestion)?
main_finding: The proposed multi-perspective framework and its instantiated distance measures (e.g., NGD, CFLD, AED, RED, CED, CWD, CAR, CTD) can discern the impact of controlled perturbations on BPS models and reveal the comparative strengths/weaknesses of two automated BPS discovery techniques (SIMOD vs. ServiceMiner); the proposed NGD measure matches CFLD's discriminative power at much lower computational cost (Kendall correlation of 1.0).
limitations: The framework only applies to BPS models that can generate event logs (not e.g. system-dynamics models), treats the actual event log as ground truth (assuming it fully represents process behavior), and the evaluation is limited to 29 synthetic and 8 real-life discovered BPS models across a few domains, limiting internal/external/construct/ecological validity generalization.

qa_notes: OCR extraction has garbled math symbols/subscripts (e.g. mangled equations, 'vr' for pi) but the methodology and results remain assessable; no explicit threats-to-validity section or data/code availability statement found.
research_question: How can Importance Sampling applied to a Markov software usage model produce an unbiased, low-variance estimator of software reliability while directing more test effort toward error-prone but infrequently used operations?
main_finding: The proposed importance-sampling learning algorithm (based on the Ali-Silvey/Kullback-Leibler distance) for optimizing Markov usage-model transition probabilities yields a reliability estimator with lower variance (8.32e-4) than the standard method (5.21e-3) and simulated annealing (1.683e-3), while giving more testing weight to critical low-frequency operations.
limitations: The approach is restricted to Markov (memoryless) usage models with manageable state-space size to avoid state-space explosion, and the zero-variance estimator is not fully achieved in practice due to statistical estimation error from finite sampling; authors note future work on non-Markov models, larger state spaces, and formal convergence proofs.

qa_notes: Text is clean and readable overall (only minor OCR artifacts in probability equations); no code/data availability statement is given beyond naming the licensed ISBSG dataset, so QA7 scored 0.
research_question: Does a 'Bellwether effect' exist in software effort estimation, and can a Markov-chain-based stratification/sampling method determine an effective window size and age for a Bellwether moving window that improves prediction accuracy over a growing-portfolio baseline?
main_finding: Using Markov chain Monte Carlo-based stratification and sampling on the ISBSG dataset, the study empirically confirms a Bellwether effect in software effort estimation and identifies an optimal Bellwether moving window of 82-84 projects with an age of 1.5-2 years (Gaussian weighting), which significantly outperforms the traditional growing-portfolio approach (Welch t-test p<0.05, Glass's Delta=0.627).
limitations: The study relies on a single release of the ISBSG dataset restricted to a single industry sector (a convenience sample), so results may not generalize to other chronological datasets; authors plan to validate the method on other datasets (e.g., a Finnish dataset) in future work.

main_finding: This research-in-progress (design science) paper proposes leveraging process mining on existing information-system logs to automatically maintain up-to-date employee knowledge/skill profiles for team selection, illustrated through an ongoing case study at software company Cegeka; no empirical results are yet reported, only research design and anticipated challenges.

research_question: How can Monte Carlo simulation and stochastic modeling of software development sub-phase efforts be used to produce confidence-based effort estimates that account for process variability, instead of deterministic estimation methods?
main_finding: Using stochastic notations and PDFs fitted from historical data of 70 real development projects, a Monte Carlo simulation tool (built on @Risk) can generate confidence-based effort estimates per SDLC phase/sub-phase, and sensitivity analysis identifies which sub-phases contribute most variability for targeted process improvement.
limitations: Authors state the model and notations were developed only for 'development' type projects (not other project types such as maintenance or migration), and that process performance varies across organizations, technologies, and personnel skills.

qa_notes: Full postprint text is clean and complete (no OCR garbling); QA2 scored 0 because the paper is a general business-process-mining/conformance-checking contribution (illustrated on healthcare, insurance, loan, and IT-incident logs) with no dedicated software-engineering context description.
research_question: How can classical precision and recall conformance-checking measures be lifted to account for the stochastic perspective of event logs and process models (e.g., Stochastic Petri nets), so that frequent versus rare deviations can be distinguished?
main_finding: The proposed entropy-based and gain-based stochastic precision/recall measures satisfy more of the desirable formal properties than existing techniques (EMSC, entropic relevance) and non-stochastic alignments, are computationally feasible on ten real-life public event logs, and successfully identified 48 pairs of near-duplicate stochastic process models in an industrial (German health insurer) repository of ~4,000 models.
limitations: The entropy measures only account for common prefixes (not postfixes) of traces, do not simultaneously consider the stochastic perspective of both log and model (the gain measures do, but ignore partial trace matches), and the approach does not yet extend to infinite-state/unbounded process models; the industrial case-study models could not be released publicly per the company agreement.

qa_notes: Full text (Springer SN Computer Science article) reads cleanly with no OCR noise; QA6/QA7/QA8 scored 0 because there is no explicit threats-to-validity discussion, the industrial CI/CD event data and code are not released, and no fitness/precision/F1-style model-quality metric is reported (only frequency counts of pipeline stage transitions).
research_question: How can Apache Kafka be used to integrate and normalize heterogeneous CI/CD event logs in near real time so that process mining (discovery/conformance) techniques can be applied to monitor and improve an organization's CI/CD workflow?
main_finding: Applying the heuristics miner to Kafka-normalized CI/CD event logs from a large e-commerce company's Jenkins/GitLab pipelines revealed a 'deceiving perception' of CI/CD as an orderly sequence: it exposed pipeline misconfigurations, undocumented/anomalous stages (e.g., builds bypassing QA/UAT), and missing metadata, demonstrating that process mining plus streaming integration gives actionable observability of real-world DevOps pipelines.
limitations: The study covers only discovery-based monitoring (Jan-May 2020) at one company's specific tool stack; full real-time conformance checking is explicitly left as future/ongoing work, and metrics such as feature-branch lead time are only available for Git/GitLab projects, not for SVN-based trunk development.

qa_notes: Short, digital-native LNCS tool-demo paper, no OCR issues; QA2 scored 0 because the tool and its three evaluation logs (purchase-to-pay, academic credentials recognition, manufacturing production) are generic business processes, not software engineering; QA8 credited because Simod quantifies similarity between simulated and real logs via a (Damerau-Levenshtein + time-penalty) distance metric functioning as a model-quality score.
research_question: Can a tool (Simod) automatically discover an accurate business process simulation model directly from an event log, by combining automated process discovery, conformance-based log repair, simulation-parameter extraction, and Bayesian hyperparameter optimization?
main_finding: Simod automatically produces BIMP-executable simulation models from an XES/MXML event log by combining SplitMiner-based control-flow discovery, trace-alignment-based conformance repair, and Bayesian-optimized parameter extraction, and was shown on one synthetic and two real-life logs to reproduce process performance measures similar to those observed in the original logs.
limitations: The accuracy of the generated simulation model is inherently limited by the accuracy of the discovered process model and by the pre-processing parameters chosen; this first version supports only the SplitMiner discovery algorithm and the BIMP simulator, with the use of multiple mining algorithms left as future work.

main_finding: Using a new explicit likelihood function that accounts for the dependency between fault detection and fault correction processes, MLE parameter estimates give more accurate and stable predictions (lower mean relative error) of future fault detection/correction behavior than least-squares estimates, confirmed on a real dataset and via Monte Carlo simulation of 120 datasets.
limitations: not stated

qa_notes: Well-structured case-study/experience-report paper with detailed dataset description and self-critique of metric limitations (entropy, gaming risk); no fitness/precision-style process-model quality metrics reported and no public dataset/code release.
research_question: How can process mining of Wiki, version-control, and issue-tracking event logs from student teams in an undergraduate SE course give instructors visibility into development-process quality (workload distribution, commit quality, bug-fixing efficiency) beyond what is visible from the product alone?
main_finding: Applying process mining (via Disco/Fuzzy Miner) and custom metrics (component/developer entropy, bug-fixing score, commit-message quality) to Wiki, VCS, and ITS logs from 19 student teams reveals large, previously invisible variation in process quality between teams, giving instructors actionable, non-product-based feedback and grading signals.
limitations: Authors note the entropy-based metrics capture diversity rather than intensity of contribution, and that all proposed metrics can be gamed by redundant/needless commits or bug reports, so should be used cautiously for grading.

qa_notes: Formal/theoretical position paper (van der Aalst) using only toy illustrative examples, no real event log, case study, or SE-specific context; no threats-to-validity discussion and no shared data/code, though fitness/precision/generalization are formally defined.
research_question: How can process discovery and conformance checking be decomposed and distributed across computing nodes (via vertical/horizontal partitioning of event logs and 'passages' of a process model) to handle large-scale event logs, for both procedural (Petri net) and declarative process models?
main_finding: The paper introduces the notion of 'passages' to decompose Petri-net-based conformance checking (and, under a known causal structure, process discovery) into independent subproblems that can each be solved on a sublog/net-fragment and then merged, proving that a log is perfectly fitting a workflow net iff each decomposed sublog is perfectly fitting its corresponding net fragment.
limitations: The paper notes horizontal distribution of procedural (Petri-net) models is much more challenging than vertical distribution or declarative models, and provides no empirical performance evaluation on real large event logs -- only illustrative toy examples.

qa_notes: This is itself a rigorous systematic literature review (SLR) with a reproducible QGS-based search protocol and kappa-checked screening, but it studies software process SIMULATION modeling (not process mining) and reports no process-model fitness/precision metrics; no dedicated threats-to-validity section for the SLR itself.
research_question: What is the state-of-the-art of software process simulation modeling (SPSM) research from 2008-2012 -- purposes, simulation paradigms, tools, and problem domains -- compared to the prior 1998-2007 review period?
main_finding: An updated SLR of 74 primary studies (2008-2012) found no significant change in the overall volume of SPSM research in the SE community versus 1998-2007, although ProSim/ICSSP-specific publications declined; System Dynamics and Discrete-Event Simulation remain the dominant paradigms, hybrid simulation is increasingly used, but many Category-A studies still lack industry-scale validation.
limitations: The authors note that many software process simulation model/simulator studies fail to trial their models on industry-scale problems, and that limitations of the paradigms/methods used are still rarely discussed in the reviewed literature; space limits also meant only RQ1-RQ4 of the planned six research questions were reported.

qa_notes: Rigorous empirical/statistical case study of a production SaaS platform's operational failures (MTBF, Laplace/Mann-Kendall trend tests, distribution fitting); no dedicated threats-to-validity section and underlying data/LOC counts are kept confidential, limiting reproducibility.
research_question: What are the common causes of operational failures in a production business-data-processing SaaS platform, and how do workload intensity and workload volume affect the platform's failure rate?
main_finding: Analysis of 283 days of operational logs from a production CPG SaaS platform found that 34.1% of failures stem from unexpected values in customer data and 32.7% from timeouts; failure rate increases with workload intensity (not workload volume) and is largely insensitive to software upgrades, with failure inter-arrival times fitting a Fatigue Life distribution that becomes exponential once timeout failures are removed.
limitations: The authors note the findings are based on a single, specific SaaS platform, so generalizability to other systems is not established, and that 29.8% of failures could not be diagnosed because they produced only empty log entries, a data-quality limitation of the underlying logs used in the study.

qa_notes: This paper is NOT about software engineering -- it is a formal-verification/control-theory tool-benchmarking competition report for stochastic hybrid/cyber-physical systems (water distribution networks, autonomous vehicles, anesthesia, building automation); QA2 (SE context) is scored 0 because there is no software-engineering process content at all. Likely a false-positive inclusion in the SE-focused SLR corpus (matched on the 'stochastic models' keyword).
research_question: How do state-of-the-art tools for formal verification and control synthesis of stochastic (hybrid) systems compare on established and newly introduced benchmarks in the 2025 ARCH-COMP friendly competition?
main_finding: The report compares six stochastic-system verification/control-synthesis tools (three new: IMPaCT, IntervalMDP.jl, PRoTECT; three established: SySCoRe, hpnmg, AMYTISS) on established and newly introduced benchmarks (including a new water distribution network benchmark), showing e.g. that the IPS-FAS algorithm greatly outperforms plain Monte Carlo simulation for rare-event collision-probability estimation, and that hpnmg's new guided-simulation engine is faster than classical discrete-event simulation on the same hybrid Petri net model.
limitations: The authors identify ongoing open challenges for the field, including high-dimensional scalability, rare-event estimation, and handling expressive specifications, which remain unresolved for the compared tools.

qa_notes: Solid experimental validation using two well-known synthetic benchmarks (TPC-W, oo7) with statistical testing (Z-test) and runtime-overhead measurement; no explicit threats-to-validity section and the instrumentation tool/code is not stated to be publicly released.
research_question: Can Markov-chain models built from observed runtime data-access sequences in object-oriented applications accurately predict future data-access patterns, to support automated data prefetching/optimization?
main_finding: A Markov-chain-based system that instruments Java applications via bytecode rewriting to learn field-level data-access patterns achieves highly accurate predictions (Z-values near zero, within 95% confidence) on the TPC-W and oo7 benchmarks, with only about 9% runtime overhead and negligible extra memory cost.
limitations: Authors note the chosen type-based (vs. instance-based) analysis approach trades some specificity for scalability, and that it can be difficult to identify which specific object instances to target for optimization once predictions are available; no formal threats-to-validity discussion is included.

qa_notes: Strong methodological paper with a discussion resembling threats to validity (accuracy of input parameters, validity of Markov modeling assumptions); the two 'empirical' case studies use illustrative/parametrized values modeled on real industrial systems rather than measured field data, and no dataset/code is shared.
research_question: How can an automated test-case-generation approach based on Markov-chain performability models (combining resource-usage and resource-failure sub-models) select a minimal set of most-probable test configurations to efficiently assess whether a large industrial system meets combined reliability and performance requirements?
main_finding: Extending prior Markov-chain-based test generation with performability theory, the paper shows on two illustrative industrial-like case studies (a distributed data-center system and a triple-redundant mission-critical system) how to select a minimal, most-probable set of resource configurations to test, computing a reliability/performance metric G(t) (fraction of time requirements are met) without exhaustively testing all configurations.
limitations: The authors explicitly note that model applicability depends on the accuracy of input parameter values and the validity of modeling assumptions, recommending sensitivity analysis as future work; full application to certify a real large mission-critical system is also left as future work.

qa_notes: Strong methodological rigor with an explicit threats-to-validity discussion (transition-probability sensitivity analysis via the FAST method, and a memorylessness robustness check); underlying process model and calibration data are not shared due to company confidentiality.
research_question: What is the economic benefit (in effort and duration) of using isolated test/development environments (Caps) versus shared/non-isolated mainframe software development, and how can this be quantified when a controlled empirical study is infeasible?
main_finding: Using an absorbing-Markov-chain process-simulation model calibrated with empirical effort data and configuration-management-derived conflict probabilities, the BMW case study found that isolated test/development environments (Caps) save about 20% of total development effort versus non-isolated shared mainframe development for projects with average program dependencies; sensitivity analysis confirmed this relative conclusion is robust to parameter uncertainty and to relaxing the Markov memorylessness assumption.
limitations: The authors explicitly identify the two major threats to validity as the difficulty of precisely determining transition probabilities and the memoryless assumption of Markov chains, addressing both via sensitivity analysis, but note they lack formal external validation and instead rely on correspondence with practitioners' experience.

qa_notes: No software-engineering-specific context (the case is a general ERP/business travel-management process, not a software process) and no threats-to-validity or reproducibility discussion; validation is limited to a single case with a small reference model (7 activities).
research_question: Can an industrial-engineering 'from-to chart' technique, adapted with new confidence/support/modified-lift evaluation metrics, be used to discover immediate-successor relations between activities from event logs and reconstruct an accurate process model?
main_finding: A hybrid process-discovery method adapting the industrial-engineering 'from-to chart' technique (with new confidence/support/modified-lift metrics) correctly reconstructs the sequence of immediate-successor activities in a real ERP travel-management process log, achieving 100% correct identification of immediate successors relative to the reference model.
limitations: Not explicitly discussed by the authors; the only stated limitation (as future work) is that the current from-to-chart approach is limited to sequential/straight-line behavior and cannot yet capture branching or loop constructs in the process model.

main_finding: The paper proposes a conceptual architecture for process-mining-based business process optimization, integrating an adapter layer for extracting business-process data, a business-knowledge representation model, and a performance-measurement system, combining macro-level (case-based reasoning) and micro-level (simulation, linear programming) optimization; no implementation or case study is provided.

research_question: Can a Hidden Markov Chain model of the software fault-detection process, which explicitly represents homogeneous 'debugging phases' via hidden states, provide better reliability predictions than standard (non-hidden) software reliability growth models when applied to real software failure datasets?
main_finding: A Hidden Markov Chain (HMM) model of software reliability, with parameters estimated via a forward-backward EM algorithm and AIC-based model selection, is compared against standard software reliability growth models (Goel-Okumoto, Musa-Okumoto, Littlewood-Verrall, etc.) on roughly 20 real software failure datasets; the HMM approach best reveals homogeneous debugging phases via its restored hidden states and gives the best predictive validity for datasets with irregular/non-monotonic reliability growth, though it performs only comparably to standard models on average and can have poor predictive validity in some cases.
limitations: The (partially legible) discussion notes that HMM predictive validity can be very poor in some cases because, in the Q-Q-plot predictive method, parameter/model estimates are computed sequentially and the selected hidden-state model can change as more data becomes available; usual (non-hidden) models perform comparably or better except when real homogeneous debugging periods and imperfect debugging are present.

qa_notes: Clean text; case study uses only a small illustrative toy log, not real-world data; no validation metrics, threats-to-validity, or reproducibility statement.
research_question: How can a matrix-based algorithm efficiently detect blocks of tasks (sets of activities with equivalent behavior) in event logs to support faster, more scalable process discovery than existing methods?
main_finding: The proposed matrix-based block discovery algorithm (using an indirect succession matrix and logical similarity operator) detects succession, parallel, XOR, and loop patterns and constructs a Petri net iteratively; the authors claim O(n^2) complexity, making it more efficient than the alpha algorithm for large event logs.
limitations: The authors state the illustrative case study log "is not representative for real-life event log in terms of size and complexity"; future work is needed to handle partial/incomplete logs.

research_question: Can Stochastic Automata Networks (SAN) offer modeling advantages (fewer states, better scalability/readability) over Markov chains for representing software usage models used in statistical testing?
main_finding: A case study modeling the DocsEditor tool with both Markov chains (53 states) and SAN (5 automata, 324 combined states but only 53 reachable) showed SAN can make implicit features (e.g., node type) explicit without state explosion, offering more modular, scalable, and maintainable usage models for statistical software testing.
limitations: The study is described as a "preliminary" and "first case study" using a relatively simple target application, focused mainly on the modeling process rather than a full framework for analysis; a full SAN-based framework and testing on more complex applications remain future work.

main_finding: Process mining of ~23,800 Chromium bug reports (using the Disco tool) revealed process inefficiencies such as fixed issues rarely being verified, frequent rework/reassignment, duplicate-status rework, and priority-handling inconsistencies (23 issues with invalid priorities), indicating the actual bug-resolution process deviates from the intended design.

research_question: Can process mining techniques (applied to event logs) be integrated into the conceptual modeling phase of Modeling & Simulation studies to produce faster, less biased, more realistic simulation models than traditional interview/observation-based conceptual modeling?
main_finding: Applying fuzzy-miner-based process mining to real Emergency Department event-log data (20,521 events, ~20,000 patients) uncovered ~90 unique patient pathways and guideline deviations; a discrete-event simulation built from the mined process closely matched real KPIs, and simulation experiments showed that resolving inpatient-bed allocation bottlenecks reduced patient length-of-stay far more (~40% at some stages) than increasing physical ED capacity.
limitations: The authors note that a cost/financial analysis of the recommendations could not be performed due to lack of cost data, and that process knowledge mined from event logs can lead to wrong conclusions due to recording errors/inaccuracies, requiring cross-validation against traditional sources before use.

qa_notes: Text has some OCR noise/garbled symbols (mathematical notation, Greek letters) typical of a scanned book chapter, but core content and examples were legible; validation relies only on small illustrative/toy programs (dining philosophers, a distributed simulator), not a real-world empirical case study.
research_question: How can Generalized Stochastic Petri Nets (GSPN), automatically generated from CSP-like distributed program code, support combined qualitative (deadlock) and quantitative (performance) static analysis of distributed software?
main_finding: The chapter presents an automatic translation procedure from CSP-like distributed program code into GSPN models, demonstrated on the dining-philosophers problem and a distributed time-warp simulator, enabling combined deadlock detection and performance-index computation (throughput, communication graphs, resource interference) without manual model construction.
limitations: The authors explicitly discuss key modeling assumptions/limitations: activity delays are assumed exponentially distributed, physical resource contention (hardware/CPU) is not modeled, and explicit representation of program variables can cause state-space explosion or even model unboundedness.

main_finding: Using Laplace transforms, matrix methods, and Runge-Kutta numerical solution, the proposed two-fault-type Markov reliability model with imperfect debugging and error generation shows reliability R(t) increasing and mean remaining faults E{D(t)} decreasing with testing time and with higher debugging/correction probabilities, supporting its use for release-time decision-making.
limitations: The authors explicitly state that no live/real failure data was available, so secondary/illustrative default parameter values were used instead of estimating parameters from actual field data.

main_finding: Preliminary case studies mining real Bugzilla bug-report histories of the Firefox and Core open-source projects (12,234 and 24,253 issues respectively) uncovered self-loops, back-and-forth transitions, and frequent reassignment/reopening, and a proposed conformance-checking algorithm found process fitness of 0.86 (Core) and 0.91 (Firefox) between the actual and the designed process.
limitations: not stated

qa_notes: Clean text; one of the most rigorous papers in this batch - real dual-project case study, named algorithms, explicit fitness metrics, and a dedicated limitations/challenges discussion, though the underlying event-log dataset itself is stated as not publicly available.
research_question: What does applying process mining (inductive-miner discovery plus token-replay conformance checking, extended with case/organizational/time perspectives) reveal about the real software development process of an SME, and how do results compare across two of its projects?
main_finding: Applying the L* process-mining methodology to two real projects of a Mexican software-development SME produced overall process fitness of 93.5% (Project 1) and 89.4% (Project 2); analysis revealed inconsistencies (e.g., issues marked Done without prior Validation), role/staff-turnover differences, and common SME-specific challenges such as documentation gaps and tool-integration difficulties.
limitations: The paper discusses several challenges: lack of process documentation, difficulty integrating heterogeneous tool records (Jira, GitHub, SIMIo), staff turnover and inadequate communication affecting model interpretation in Project 2, and explicitly states the underlying event-log dataset is not publicly available due to privacy.

qa_notes: Clean text; rigorous methodological paper with an open, downloadable running-example dataset and tool (ProM) and two real-life case studies, but the empirical case studies are municipal government processes (complaint/invoice handling), not a software engineering process, so QA2 scored low.
research_question: Can multiple process-mining perspectives (control-flow, data, performance, organizational) be automatically discovered from event logs and integrated into a single Colored Petri Net simulation model that accurately reproduces the original process's behavior?
main_finding: Combining control-flow, decision, performance, and organizational-perspective process mining into an integrated Colored Petri Net simulation model (via the ProM/CPN Tools pipeline) allowed automatic simulation-model discovery; a "second pass" evaluation on an artificial running example and two real-life Dutch municipality case studies (complaint handling, invoice handling) showed the generated models reproduced the original control-flow, data, and performance characteristics with high fidelity (e.g., 100% fitness).
limitations: The authors note that human/resource behavior is imperfectly captured because people work part-time across multiple concurrent processes, requiring an ad hoc addition of extra waiting time that does not truly reflect real working patterns; they also note the evaluation approach does not address the validity of the underlying log data itself.

qa_notes: Clean text; the most thorough and rigorous document in this batch (full MSc dissertation) - real open-source case studies, explicit precision/recall metrics, dedicated threats-to-validity and limitations sections, and open-source underlying tools/data.
research_question: Can a process-mining-based approach (Reuse Miner) automatically discover object-oriented framework instantiation processes from existing application source code, represented executably in the Reuse Description Language (RDL)?
main_finding: Reuse Miner, applying heuristics-miner process discovery and RPST-based translation to event logs mined from GEF and Graphiti framework applications (including GitHub-sourced repositories), successfully generated executable RDL instantiation processes with generally high precision/recall against manually created reference processes, though results degraded (overfitting/"spaghetti" processes) when input applications were too few or too heterogeneous.
limitations: The dissertation includes a dedicated Threats to Validity section covering the manual construction of reference RDL scripts, a small/non-diverse sample of input applications causing overfitting, and the subjectivity of the precision/recall penalty factor; the Limitations/Future Work section also notes the pipeline requires substantial manual interaction with the ProM tool and does not fully automate repeated process discovery across sub-processes.

qa_notes: PDF text extraction used a garbled custom font encoding (fixed via a uniform +29 ASCII-shift decode) but content was fully readable once decoded; paper is about CEP+ML for financial streaming analytics, not process mining/stochastic modeling in software engineering, so QA2/QA4/QA8 are largely inapplicable to the SLR's intended domain.
research_question: How can complex event processing (CEP) and machine learning be integrated into a single open architecture to preprocess real-time data streams and support downstream ML training/prediction, demonstrated via stock-price pattern detection?
main_finding: The proposed open architecture (Kafka + EventSwarm CEP + TensorFlow) successfully combines CEP-based event pattern detection with ML training/prediction in two demonstrated real-time stock-analysis scenarios (LSTM price prediction and DTW-based pairs-trading pattern matching), showing that CEP preprocessing improves the relevance of features fed to ML models.
limitations: Authors note the need for an additional data-transformation component to match input requirements across different ML algorithms, that retraining frequency/dataset growth trades off compute cost against accuracy, and that continuous learning and broader CEP/ML algorithm support are left as future work.

qa_notes: Detailed, well-structured reliability-modeling paper with an explicit dedicated Threats-to-Validity section (4.4); not a process-mining paper, no code/data repository provided, and reported accuracy/deviation metrics are reliability-prediction accuracy rather than PM-style fitness/precision metrics.
research_question: How can a 'component influence' metric combined with a global state-transition model (based on a discrete-time Markov chain) more accurately assess component-based software system reliability than existing architecture-based methods, while accounting for the diversity of software architectural styles?
main_finding: On a benchmark bank-transaction software system case study, the proposed component-influence + Markov-chain reliability model achieved a reliability estimate of 0.853 versus an actual measured reliability of 0.865 (1.39% deviation), outperforming six existing reliability-assessment methods (Cheung, Xie et al., Li and Hoang, Xue et al., Lo et al., Wang et al.) in accuracy.
limitations: Authors' own Threats to Validity section notes: the weight coefficients (alpha1, alpha2) may not generalize across all software systems; components are assumed independent, which may not hold; the model has only been validated on limited system types/architectures; comparison is limited to three classic reliability models; and predictive power across broader scenarios needs further evaluation.

qa_notes: Formal/technical stochastic Petri net paper with a detailed illustrative case study (Geldzin DevOps workflow) and simulation via TimeNET, but no dedicated threats-to-validity section and no public code/data repository for the proposed NM-WSPN model itself (only the case study's tools/blog reference are public).
research_question: How can a non-Markovian stochastic Petri net extension (NM-WSPN) formally specify, verify (liveness/boundedness/soundness), and predict duration/delay risk of DevOps workflows, capturing dynamic interactions between developer and operator actors?
main_finding: Applying the proposed NM-WSPN model to the Geldzin DevOps case study (steps 9-17 of a real CI/CD pipeline) revealed a blocking state (CardM15) and identified transition Tr14 as the primary source of delay; density-truncation-based prediction estimated delay margins and confidence intervals for critical transitions (e.g., ~60% probability of continuous delay under an exponential firing-time distribution for transition Tr21).
limitations: The model assumes independence between activity durations, is demonstrated on a single illustrative case study rather than broad empirical validation, and future work is needed to add resource-sharing constraints and dynamic real-time verification capabilities; no formal threats-to-validity discussion is included.

qa_notes: This is a doctoral-symposium/work-in-progress paper (ICSE 2016 Companion) describing an ongoing research proposal rather than a completed empirical study; most of the described framework (conformance, enhancement phases, full evaluation) is future work, and no code/data repository or threats-to-validity section is provided.
research_question: How can process mining techniques (discovery, conformance, enhancement) be extended to work with Software Process Lines (families of related process variants) rather than single processes, particularly to help small software enterprises (SSEs) capture and improve their real, often-undocumented development processes?
main_finding: This work-in-progress paper proposes an end-to-end Process Mining framework (discovery, conformance, enhancement) for Software Process Lines and reports a prototype discovery algorithm ('v-algorithm', implemented as a ProM plug-in) already applied to event logs extracted from 2 of 5 target Chilean small software enterprises via a descriptive case study, with results manually compared to the companies' known processes; conformance and enhancement components remain future work.
limitations: The paper is explicitly an early-stage/ongoing research proposal without full empirical validation: only 2 of 5 target companies had event logs extracted so far, conformance/enhancement prototypes are not yet built, and planned evaluation with company stakeholders had not yet been conducted at time of writing.

qa_notes: Very thorough empirical process-mining + ML case study (Empirical Software Engineering journal) with a dedicated Threats-to-Validity section (Sec. 11) and survey triangulation; raw ticket data itself is confidential/not shared (company policy), though keyword lists, process models, and anonymized survey results were published on GitHub; QA8=0 because reported precision/recall are for ML classifiers, not process-model conformance metrics.
research_question: How can process mining and machine learning be used to analyze and reduce real and tactical (non-information-seeking) user input requests in IT support ticket resolution, thereby shortening the gap between measured service-level resolution time and user-experienced resolution time?
main_finding: Process mining of 593,497 real IT support tickets from a large global IT company showed 57% of tickets have at least one 'Awaiting User Input' state, making user-experienced resolution time roughly double the measured service-level time; an SVM-based preemptive model achieved 94-99% accuracy (vs 50-60% for naive Bayes/logistic regression baselines) at anticipating needed information, and a rule-based detection model identified about 15% of input requests as tactical.
limitations: Authors' Threats to Validity section notes: findings on tactical requests may not generalize to organizations with different characteristics (external validity); the preemptive model was evaluated on held-out test data, not in live production (conclusion validity); and communication occurring outside the ticketing system (phone/chat) was not observable, potentially affecting the preemptive model (construct validity).

qa_notes: Rigorous ML/process-mining experimental paper with public code (GitHub: raseidi/cosmo) and public BPI benchmark datasets; limitations are discussed in a dedicated subsection (5.3) though not formally titled 'Threats to Validity'; QA2=0 because the evaluated event logs (BPI12/13/17/20, SEPSIS) are general business/healthcare processes rather than software-engineering-specific processes.
research_question: How can deep-learning-based process simulation models be conditioned on user-defined declarative (DECLARE/LTLf) constraints to overcome the inherent stochasticity and lack of controllability of existing DL-based simulation approaches, enabling what-if analysis?
main_finding: CoSMo, a novel conditioned recurrent neural architecture incorporating DECLARE/LTLf constraints into deep-learning process simulation, achieves high weighted precision (median 99% when replaying original rules, 81% under inverted/what-if constraints) across five real-world BPI event logs, substantially outperforming an unconstrained 'vanilla' stochastic baseline (~58% precision) in controlling simulated process behavior.
limitations: Authors note correlated DECLARE rules (e.g., existence/absence) may introduce redundant information, rule/activity selection was performed arbitrarily without domain-expert input, and the study only explored declarative/LTLf constraints rather than other constraint types (e.g., resource- or time-based), limiting real-world applicability so far.

qa_notes: Theoretical/algorithmic conformance-checking paper (PNSE'16) with formal proofs plus computational benchmarking on public BPI Challenge and other public event-log datasets; QA2=0 since it is a generic process-mining algorithms paper without a specific software-engineering process context; no code repository or threats-to-validity section provided.
research_question: How does decomposed replay for process-mining conformance checking behave computationally compared to monolithic replay, and can an alternative 'hide-and-reduce' decomposition avoid cases where decomposed replay is slower than monolithic replay while still providing better lower-bound cost estimates?
main_finding: Decomposed replay can, in some cases (especially with discovered nets containing subnets with several source transitions), take far longer than monolithic replay; the proposed 'hide-and-reduce' alternative decomposition avoids this misbehavior (finishing within 10 minutes for nearly all tested cases) and typically produces tighter (better) lower-bound cost estimates than the original decomposed replay, though it can be slower due to the added reduction step.
limitations: The reduction step itself can become a computational bottleneck (up to ~60 seconds in some cases even when the underlying replay takes only 2 seconds), and the proposed method is sometimes slower than the original decomposed replay; no formal threats-to-validity discussion is provided.

qa_notes: Theoretical control-theory/automata paper (American Control Conference 2003) applying semi-Markov reward processes and 'language measure' theory to a software rejuvenation example; the numeric illustration reuses parameter values from a cited prior study rather than original data collection, so there is no real empirical validation, reproducibility statement, or threats-to-validity discussion.
research_question: How can a signed real 'language measure' of automata (extended from discrete-time Markov chains to semi-Markov reward processes) be used to formally analyze and optimize software rejuvenation (preventive restart) policies for improving software availability/performance?
main_finding: Extending the language-measure approach from discrete-time Markov chains to semi-Markov reward processes enables analytical comparison and optimization of software rejuvenation policies (level-1 partial restart vs level-2 full restart); applying sojourn-time estimates from prior literature, the analysis concludes the optimal policy is pure level-2 (full) restart, consistent with an earlier study's finding obtained via a different (deterministic) method.
limitations: The analysis is purely theoretical/illustrative, relying on numeric parameters borrowed from a prior paper rather than new empirical measurement; the paper provides no discussion of threats to validity or real-system validation.

qa_notes: Primarily a theoretical/simulation paper (MATLAB numeric example with assumed/simulated parameter values on a hypothetical component-based system) rather than an empirical case study with real measured data; no threats-to-validity section or code/data availability statement.
research_question: How can a Markov chain-based error propagation model, using only per-component and pairwise integration-testing data, estimate the reliability of an entire component-based software system without full system-level testing, while also supporting fault localization and critical-component protection?
main_finding: The proposed Markov-based error propagation model (using only 4n-2 states versus the exponential 2^n states of a comparable prior model) can estimate component and system reliability, localize the most likely fault-causing component, and identify critical components needing protection; demonstrated via a MATLAB simulation on a 7-component 'Make to Order' production-planning system example, achieving a computed path reliability of 0.8989.
limitations: Authors state the current model only considers transient states (future work will add absorbing states), compatibility across different system structures remains a challenge, and obtaining reliable probability distributions for path selection needs improved methods; no real empirical/industrial validation was performed, only a simulated numeric example with assumed parameters.

qa_notes: Purely theoretical/mathematical software-reliability-modeling paper (ISSRE 2002) with no empirical case study, real dataset, threats-to-validity discussion, or code/data availability; the paper explicitly defers practical parameter estimation and application to real data to future work.
research_question: How can a unifying differential-equation framework and a vector Markov model (extending existing software reliability growth models) formally relate test-case execution, structural code-coverage growth (allowing partial redundancy), and the expected number of failure occurrences?
main_finding: The paper develops a 'vector Markov model' for structural coverage growth that generalizes and bridges existing operational-testing (Piwowarski et al.) and systematic-testing (Rivers-Vouk) coverage models by allowing partial redundancy in code-construct sampling, and shows two extensions of this model (fault detection at first vs. repeated construct execution) both reduce to special cases of an overarching differential-equation framework unifying several classical software reliability growth models (Goel-Okumoto, Jelinski-Moranda, ENHPP).
limitations: The paper explicitly states it focuses only on theoretical model derivation; practical parameter estimation and application to real software development/testing data are described as 'the subject of the current research activities' (future work), with no dataset applied in this paper.

qa_notes: Well-known process-mining/software-engineering paper demonstrating the ProM framework on real ArgoUML SVN logs; tools (ProM, ProMImport) and the ArgoUML repository are publicly available, but no explicit numeric process-model quality metrics (fitness/precision) or dedicated threats-to-validity section are reported.
research_question: How can process mining techniques and the ProM framework be applied to Software Configuration Management (SCM) system logs (e.g., Subversion/CVS) to automatically discover, analyze, and verify explicit software development process models across control-flow, organizational, and informational perspectives?
main_finding: Applying the ProM process mining framework (via a two-step transition-system-generation-and-Petri-net-synthesis approach, plus Alpha/Heuristics/Genetic Miner alternatives) to real Subversion commit logs from the ArgoUML open-source project produced plausible software-development process models, and enabled further performance analysis, conformance checking, LTL-based rule checking, and social network analysis of developer collaboration (e.g., detecting a developer who both wrote source code and tests, violating a separation-of-duties constraint).
limitations: The generation-and-synthesis approach struggles to handle noise (incorrectly logged events/exceptions) in the log; the paper demonstrates the tool/methodology on a single project rather than providing a broad empirical validation, and no formal threats-to-validity discussion is included.

qa_notes: Forward-looking position/proposal paper (ENASE 2013) describing planned future research phases (initiation, implementation, testing, evaluation) rather than reporting completed empirical work; the authors explicitly state drawing conclusions now would be 'premature and risky', so most QA criteria requiring data, validation, or reproducibility are unmet by design.
research_question: How can a novel 'Intelligent Agile Method Framework' (iAMF) — combining situational method engineering with process/intention mining of developers' real actions via revision-control-system logs — help software companies capture, follow, and continuously improve the development methods they actually use in practice, raising process maturity and reducing project failures?
main_finding: This position/research-proposal paper introduces the 'Intelligent Agile Method Framework' (iAMF) concept and toolset architecture, which aims to mine developers' actual revision-control-system actions to document a company's real 'base method,' detect and guide deviations from it, and iteratively raise software process maturity toward CMMI levels 3-5; no empirical results are reported, as evaluation had not yet been conducted at time of writing.
limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge the research is longitudinal and evaluation-dependent, with no empirical results available at time of publication; the framework had not yet been tested or evaluated with real companies, and hypotheses (H1-H4) about developer adoption and maturity improvement remain unconfirmed.

qa_notes: Concrete real-world case study (Robin's Nest health platform) with clear objectives and SE/agile context, but no reproducible dataset details (no case/event counts), no explicitly named PM discovery algorithm actually applied, no formal threats-to-validity discussion, no data/code availability, and no process-model quality metrics.
research_question: How can process mining insights from Jira/GitHub data be used to identify deficiencies in multidisciplinary agile requirements engineering, and can an automated effort-estimation tool reduce change requests and improve release planning?
main_finding: Communication gaps and lack of domain knowledge among multidisciplinary stakeholders caused high rework rates and requirement changes; an NLP (BERT)-based effort-estimation decision-support tool helped reduce the backlog of remaining user stories.
limitations: Plurality of stakeholders and non-technical stakeholders' lack of software engineering knowledge are cited as causes of inefficiency; authors plan to adopt formal process mining tools (ProM, Disco) in future work, implying the current analysis was not based on standard PM discovery techniques.

qa_notes: Well-described CPN simulation model plus a real-life event log (324 cases, 19805 events, 15 resources, 175 activities) with regression fit statistics (r, R2); no formal threats-to-validity section and no explicit code/data release statement.
research_question: How can workload-dependent processing speeds of resources be incorporated into simulation models and learned from event logs using process mining, and does workload measurably affect resource processing speed in real life?
main_finding: Simulation experiments (colored Petri nets) and regression analysis of a real-life municipal permit-handling event log both confirm that resource workload (queue length and 'how busy' measures) significantly affects processing speed, following a Yerkes-Dodson-like relationship; ignoring this yields unrealistic simulation results.
limitations: The model only captures the first half of the Yerkes-Dodson curve (busier resources work faster) and does not model other resource behaviors such as multitasking, part-time availability, or batch working, which the authors address only in separate earlier work.

qa_notes: Rigorous formal/simulation study on self-adaptive systems (Rainbow framework) with explicit statement that Matlab source code and data are publicly available; no formal threats-to-validity discussion and no process-mining-style quality metrics (this is an MDP decision-accuracy study, not process discovery).
research_question: How can an iterative decision-making scheme infer point and interval estimates of transition probabilities in a Markov Decision Process from runtime data and trade off accuracy, data usage, and computational overhead when selecting a confidently optimal scheduler for self-adaptive systems?
main_finding: The proposed Iterative Decision-Making Scheme (IDMS), embedded into the Rainbow self-adaptation framework, flexibly trades off accuracy, data usage, and computational overhead, achieving higher correctness rates than simple point estimation (especially for larger sample sizes), as shown via Monte Carlo simulation on a Rainbow-based example system.
limitations: Future work is needed to automatically adjust the confident-optimality criterion and sample size based on given metric priorities, and to generalize the value-iteration method so it can synthesize a scheduler without requiring a predefined, restricted subset of schedulers.

qa_notes: Real software systems (developed by one of the authors) are used for validation with named high-order Markov chain techniques and AIC/BIC order-selection criteria, but the datasets/logs themselves are not shared or fully described for independent reproduction; no formal threats-to-validity discussion.
research_question: Can discrete- and continuous-time high-order Markov chain models, which account for dependencies among software component runs, provide more accurate software reliability assessment than standard first-order Markov chain models?
main_finding: High-order Markov chain models increase software reliability assessment accuracy by up to 6% (discrete-time) and 10-20% (continuous-time) compared to first-order models, by better capturing interdependence among software component runs; the optimal chain order is determined via AIC/BIC criteria.
limitations: Practical aspects of estimating model input parameters and studying how reliability depends on software characteristics (component count, variables per component, component cohesion, etc.) are explicitly deferred to future work.

qa_notes: Purely theoretical formal-methods paper (extension of Hybrid CSP with stochastic differential equations and an extended Hoare Logic); only a toy illustrative aircraft example is used, with no real case study, dataset, reproducibility artifact, or threats-to-validity discussion.
research_question: How can Hybrid CSP be extended with probabilistic choice and stochastic differential equations to model stochastic hybrid systems (SHCSP), and how can Hybrid Hoare Logic be extended to formally specify and verify probability-related properties of such processes?
main_finding: The paper defines Stochastic HCSP (SHCSP) with a well-defined operational semantics (proven measurable and adapted to a Markov-time filtration) and a compositional Hoare-Logic-based proof system for reasoning about probability of properties, illustrated on an aircraft flight-path safety example.
limitations: Not explicitly stated; the authors note as motivation that existing probabilistic model-checking techniques for SHSs do not scale (e.g., for SDEs with more than two variables), but do not present a limitations section evaluating their own deductive approach's scope or restrictions.

qa_notes: This is a special-panel position/discussion paper about the state of Software Process Simulation research, not an empirical study; virtually all empirical-rigor QA criteria are inapplicable, so a uniformly low QA score is expected and appropriate.
research_question: What are the challenges facing Software Process Simulation (SPS) research and practice given its apparent stagnation, and what research agenda and collaborations could help SPS achieve broader industrial adoption and impact?
main_finding: This panel paper reports no empirical findings; it frames a discussion on SPS's slowing growth and sets goals to identify challenges, propose solutions, and develop a future SPS research agenda involving both academia and industry panelists.
limitations: Not applicable; this is a panel position paper rather than an empirical study, so no limitations of an empirical method are discussed.

qa_notes: Solid two-project case study with an explicit limitations discussion, but no formally named process-mining discovery algorithm, no shared/reproducible dataset, and no process-model quality metrics reported.
research_question: Do software architecture (module dependency) and technical development process factors significantly influence fine-grained micro-process activities, their cost, and recurring patterns, beyond what macro-process methodologies capture?
main_finding: Mining micro-processes from time sheets in two commercial projects, combined with architecture reconstruction (JDepend, SA4J) and structured interviews, confirmed that both architectural module dependency and technology-specific development processes strongly influence which micro-process activities occur, their cost, and recurring patterns.
limitations: The authors explicitly note that (1) only two of many possible influencing factors (Figure 1) were studied and other factors may play a more dominant role, and (2) the study only observed after-the-fact effects rather than actively using these factors in process planning.

qa_notes: Rigorous formal/simulation study with fully specified synthetic input parameters (means, variances, coupling scenarios) enabling manual reproduction of the sample computations; no explicit code/data release, no formal threats-to-validity discussion, and no process-mining-style quality metrics (reports optimal cost/duration instead).
research_question: How can feedback between software development activities (rework caused by design changes and component coupling) be formalized as a Markov Decision Process to compute optimal team-scheduling strategies that minimize expected project cost/duration?
main_finding: Using an MDP-based software process scheduling model, optimal strategies were computed for a sample project via value iteration; results show optimal project cost/duration increases with the strength of inter-component coupling and decreases when teams are specialized on particular components.
limitations: Not explicitly stated as a limitations section; the model assumes an acyclic MDP state space and relies on statistical data about past projects plus high-level design coupling information as required inputs, which is presented as a modeling requirement rather than an acknowledged limitation.

qa_notes: Strong empirical and reproducibility profile: public code/data repository, quantitative accuracy metrics (EMD, KS, 3-gram), and evaluation on both real (Traffic, Sepsis, BPIC19) and 150 synthetic event logs; no explicit threats-to-validity section, though scope limitations are stated as future work.
research_question: How can data-aware business process simulation models — including global, case, and event attribute update rules and data-driven branching conditions — be automatically discovered from event logs, and do they more accurately replicate real process control flow than data-unaware simulation models?
main_finding: The proposed discovery method accurately classifies data attribute types and their update rules (about 95% correct classification) and the resulting data-aware simulation models replicate process execution control flow more accurately than data-unaware baseline models, particularly for case-based attributes and OR-gateway scenarios.
limitations: The approach only discovers update rules where an attribute's new value depends on that same attribute's own previous value (not on multiple attributes jointly), does not model data-dependent activity durations, and does not handle multitasking behavior, all left as future work.

qa_notes: Empirically solid study using a real, citable open-source dataset (Google Chromium issue log) with clear quantitative metrics (MAE, accuracy); no explicit threats-to-validity discussion and no stated code/data release for the extended (crawled) dataset used in this specific study.
research_question: Does incorporating case attributes (in addition to event attributes) and different categorical variable encoding techniques improve prediction of remaining issue-handling duration and next activity in software issue-tracking processes?
main_finding: Using case attributes alongside event attributes improves next-activity prediction accuracy by 8.57% and remaining-duration prediction by 1.9%; one-hot encoding (and sum encoding) achieved the best overall predictive performance (MAE 19.72 days for duration; 65.38% accuracy for next activity) on the Google Chromium issue-tracking log.
limitations: The original public dataset lacked case attributes, requiring the authors to supplement it via manual web crawling; future work is suggested to use additional predictor attributes (e.g., component, resource) and to evaluate on other data sources.

qa_notes: Purely theoretical/mathematical paper with only illustrative toy numeric examples (no real testing data or empirical case study); no reproducibility artifacts or threats-to-validity discussion.
research_question: Under the controlled Markov chains (CMC) approach to software testing, does the resulting optimal test profile (the sequence of chosen test actions) itself form a Markov chain, given that the corresponding software state transitions do?
main_finding: The paper proves that while software state transitions under an optimal CMC testing strategy always form a Markov chain, the optimal test profile (sequence of actions) is Markovian only under specific structural conditions (e.g., a contiguous block of states at the start or end mapping to one identical action while all other states map to unique actions); otherwise it is generally non-Markovian.
limitations: The authors state that the general non-Markovian conclusion for cases not satisfying the identified structural conditions 'needs further mathematical justification,' indicating the analysis is not fully proven for all cases.

qa_notes: Illustrative application of multiple stochastic process-calculus verification tools to a fully specified synthetic Finance Case-Study; case study parameters are transparently given enabling reproduction of the formal analysis, but there is no real-world dataset, no explicit code repository link in this paper, and no formal threats-to-validity discussion.
research_question: How can stochastic process calculi (MarCaSPiS, sCOWS, PEPA) and their associated quantitative analysis tools (exact and statistical model checking, stochastic probes) be used to analyze non-functional properties — performance, workload, and reactivity — of a service-oriented credit-request business process?
main_finding: Tools developed within the Sensoria Project successfully performed exact and statistical stochastic model checking and stochastic-probe querying on the Finance Case-Study credit request scenario, showing how client rating distributions affect system performance, quantifying supervisor/clerk workload and system reactivity, and demonstrating that statistical (simulation-based) model checking scales better than exact model checking as state spaces grow.
limitations: The analyzed scenario poses a 'stiff' multi-scale numerical problem because activity rates differ by several orders of magnitude (seconds vs. days), which the authors note challenges the underlying numerical routines of the quantitative analysis tools; no separate limitations section is otherwise given.

qa_notes: Clean text extraction; no formal threats-to-validity section, though authors acknowledge the constant-event-rate assumption was 'overly simplistic' in discussion.
research_question: How can internal and external software failure costs be structured and modeled using continuous-time Markov chain / Markov reward models to predict future costs?
main_finding: Using CTMC/Markov reward models built from activities, events and trigger probabilities, the approach successfully predicted internal and external failure costs in two industrial case studies, with most actual costs falling within the 95% prediction intervals.
limitations: Authors note the assumption of constant event rates was overly simplistic since fault detection rates change over time; future work is needed on parameter estimation without prior release data and on combining the model with appraisal costs.

qa_notes: Conceptual/architecture 'initial study' paper without empirical evaluation; text extraction clean, no OCR issues.
research_question: How can a semi-automatic framework be built to generate Petri net simulation models from process/event data for operational analytics, incorporating distributed processing for large data volumes?
main_finding: The paper presents an architecture (model integration, simulator engine, REST API, UI engine) combining a process-mining tool (BAB) with CPNTools for semi-automated Petri net simulation model generation from event logs; no empirical evaluation is provided.
limitations: Authors state remaining challenges include scaling the simulation engine, partitioning response files to avoid browser freezing during heavy loading, and reducing network transfer time; these are left for future work.

qa_notes: Clean text, no OCR issues; explicit 'Threats to Validity' section present (New Ideas paper with preliminary evaluation).
research_question: How can constraints for runtime monitoring of systems-of-systems be automatically mined from event logs, combining ideas from specification mining, process mining and machine learning?
main_finding: A four-step approach (sequence trees, feature vectors, decision tree/rule learning, ranking) automatically mined 43 candidate constraints from real industrial event logs of an automation systems-of-systems; engineers rated 11 of the top 15 ranked constraints as useful for monitoring.
limitations: Authors note the preliminary evaluation used small event logs from only one system, scalability was not tested at larger scale, generalizability to other systems remains to be investigated, and the learning step requires labeled valid/invalid event logs which may not always be available.

qa_notes: Clean text extraction with formulas well preserved; no explicit threats-to-validity discussion, typical of a mathematical modeling paper.
research_question: How can software safety be assessed by modeling correlated types of software errors (critical/major/minor) using a subordinated Markov chain (NHPP + DTMC), and does this model fit and predict data better than existing independent-NHPP-based models?
main_finding: Using real testing data on critical/major/minor software errors from the Shuttle Ground System, the proposed subordinated Markov chain model achieved better AIC and prediction accuracy (SAE) than two existing superposed NHPP models, yielding a more optimistic (higher) software safety estimate.
limitations: Authors note that Newton's method for estimating LPe parameters can yield invalid (negative) parameter values, and that DTMC estimation under grouped data is harder than under fully observed transition data; future work will extend the model to the software release problem.

qa_notes: Text extraction generally clean aside from minor OCR/ligature artifacts in some formulas; no dedicated threats-to-validity discussion.
research_question: How can software reliability growth modeling be improved by incorporating failure loss (severity) into the traditional J-M Markov model, creating a new 'software strong reliability' measure (SSRGM)?
main_finding: The authors propose SSRGM, extending the J-M Markov reliability model with failure loss speed instead of failure time; applied to the NTDS dataset, the model's predicted total failure loss (76.5) approximated the actual value (56), which the authors interpret as validating correctness and effectiveness.
limitations: Authors acknowledge that the experimental data used (NTDS) was originally collected for traditional reliability models, not failure-loss models, making it difficult to fully verify their model's effectiveness; collecting appropriate failure-loss data is noted as future work.

main_finding: The proposed method, combining Inductive-Miner-based trace replay (control flow) with LSTM-predicted data context, outperforms most state-of-the-art neural-network-based activity suffix prediction methods on real-life event logs (Helpdesk, Sepsis, BPIC2012W) as measured by Damerau-Levenshtein similarity, though performance degrades on datasets with low trace diversity or many self-loops.

research_question: What are the relative strengths and weaknesses of static versus dynamic architecture conformance checking approaches (RQ1), and how can the two be combined to obtain complementary synergies (RQ2)?
main_finding: Based on a theoretical comparison and a six-month industrial case study (125k-LOC Java OSGi system), static and dynamic architecture conformance checking are complementary: static (Sonargraph-Architect) is complete, fast and low-effort but limited to static structure, while dynamic (ARAMIS/Dynatrace) captures run-time behavior but is incomplete and resource-intensive (13-33 hours vs. under a minute); authors recommend static as baseline with dynamic on demand.
limitations: Authors explicitly note that their practical results are based on a single software system case study, so findings cannot be generalized, and recommend studying additional industrial cases in future work to validate the results.

qa_notes: Clean text extraction; combines system-level Markov dependability model with software reliability growth models (Littlewood-Verrall, Geometric); explicit limitations section discusses test-data quality and the heisenbug/randomness assumption, but no data/code availability and no fitness/precision-style model quality metric is reported (only availability/downtime figures).
research_question: How can system-level Markov dependability models be combined with software reliability growth models (Littlewood-Verrall, Geometric) to predict system availability/reliability and support test-time-vs-redundancy tradeoff decisions?
main_finding: Combining software reliability growth models with a system-level Markov dependability model (applied to an FAA air-traffic-control STARS example) shows diminishing returns from additional testing on system availability; e.g., ~900 extra hours of RDP testing reduces yearly downtime by only ~0.45 hours, letting managers trade off testing against redundancy/hardware reliability.
limitations: Authors note validity depends on proper operational-profile-based test data gathering, and the heisenbug/stochastic-failure assumption does not cover deterministic failures such as design flaws or security issues.

main_finding: Applying the PRICED process-mining methodology to a university Electronic Document Management System (EXPE+) revealed process-alignment deviations and data-quality challenges (non-standardized/process-independent activity names, missing timestamps, missing end-of-process events) that map to concrete software evolution actions such as renaming/standardizing activities and enforcing timestamp logging.
limitations: Authors state this is only an initial/exploratory experience with a single EDMS case, findings are not generalizable, and further validation with business experts and additional cases is needed.

research_question: How can Discrete-Time Markov Chain modeling combined with probabilistic Computation Tree Logic (pCTL) model checking be used to quantitatively and transparently analyze GitHub repository activity, branch management, and participant collaboration patterns?
main_finding: Applying DTMC-based probabilistic model checking (via PRISM) to five OSLabs GitHub repositories reveals repository-specific action rates, branch-usage patterns, pull-request processing speed, and participant contribution/merge dynamics, offering an interpretable alternative to black-box time-series/ML methods for informing project-management decisions.
limitations: Authors note the method may face challenges with repositories having complex multi-level branching strategies and could encounter state-explosion issues at larger scale (tested feasible up to ~400 participants); the study focuses on small/medium team projects rather than large-scale open-source projects.

main_finding: The mapping study identified 25 relevant papers showing process mining in agile contexts is used mainly for process discovery (via issue trackers and software repositories), with conformance checking and improvement as secondary purposes; ProM is the dominant tool and diverse algorithms (alpha, heuristic, fuzzy, genetic miners) are used, while data collection and concept drift remain key open challenges.

main_finding: The thesis proposes a framework (object generation, behavioral modeling, performance/resource modeling) for object-centric process simulation; a proof-of-concept discovering OCim models from event data showed empirical validity via conformance, object-similarity, and cycle-time measures, though components such as attribute-sensitive object generation, refined behavioral/resource modeling, and recommender systems remain open future work.

qa_notes: Clean text, encoded operation IDs in tables slightly cluttered but assessment straightforward; validation uses frequency-coverage comparison against log/Markov baselines rather than a formal fitness/precision/error metric, so QA8 scored 0; dataset is stated as freely available for research purposes (QA7=1).
research_question: Can a temporal-motifs recovery and configuration method generate software reliability test cases for updated software that adequately cover operations newly introduced by updates, compared with log-based Markov usage models that cannot cover such new operations?
main_finding: The proposed temporal-motifs recovery and configuration method generates reliability test cases whose operation-coverage frequencies are similar to those from a Markov usage model, while additionally covering operations newly introduced by software updates, which pure log-based Markov models cannot cover.
limitations: Authors note volatility from large changes in user behavior and cases where an operation absent from the immediately preceding version's log causes inaccurate coverage; they plan execution-based verification and use of more historical logs in future work.

qa_notes: Text read in full including references; this paper does not employ any process-mining algorithm or stochastic model (it is a keyword-search plus manual qualitative-coding study of code review comments), so QA4 and QA8 scored 0 — likely a borderline/tangential inclusion for a process-mining + stochastic-modeling SLR; has a formal Threats-to-Validity section and a public replication package.
research_question: What are the characteristics (categories, linguistic patterns) of architecture violation symptoms discussed in code review comments, and how do developers address them?
main_finding: Analysis of 606 code review comments from four OSS projects (Nova, Neutron, Qt Base, Qt Creator) identified three categories/ten subcategories of architecture violation symptoms (mostly design-related, especially structural inconsistencies), expressed mainly via 'inconsistent'/'violate' terms and Problem-Discovery linguistic patterns, with about 90% of symptoms addressed through refactoring or code removal regardless of patch merge status.
limitations: Authors note limited generalizability since only four OSS projects (Python/C++, OpenStack/Qt) were studied, and a construct-validity threat around the completeness of the keyword set used to identify violation-related comments.

qa_notes: Full text read including references; no process-mining or stochastic-modeling technique is used (the paper is about fault-injection-driven design of a rule-based logging mechanism, evaluated with recall/precision), so QA4 scored 0 — likely a borderline/tangential inclusion for a PM+stochastic-modeling SLR; LogBus framework code is publicly linked (sourceforge), supporting partial reproducibility.
research_question: Can a rule-based logging approach, derived from system design artifacts, significantly improve the ability of event logs to detect and report software failures compared to traditional ad-hoc logging mechanisms?
main_finding: Across roughly 12,500 fault-injection experiments on Apache webserver and TAO Open DDS, the proposed rule-based logging mechanism achieved much higher failure-detection recall (0.91-0.94 vs. 0.34-0.42 for traditional logs) with comparable or higher precision, while producing far more compact logs (up to ~275x smaller), at an acceptable runtime performance overhead (under about 16%).
limitations: Authors note rule-based logs may miss some failure-cause details (partially mitigated via a free-text complaint field) and that the approach's applicability depends on the availability of design artifacts, though reverse engineering can substitute for missing artifacts.

qa_notes: Clean, complete text; core technique (K-means/Word2Vec clustering plus naive Bayes classifier) is a machine-learning classification method that prepares SVN logs for process mining rather than a classic PM discovery/conformance algorithm or classic stochastic model; precision/recall/F-measure are reported (QA8=1) but no data/code availability statement is given (QA7=0).
research_question: Can a naive Bayes classifier, trained on K-means/Word2Vec-derived semantic clusters, automatically and incrementally map SVN log events to software process activities in real time, given the absence of native activity labels in software configuration management logs?
main_finding: The proposed K-means+Word2Vec clustering combined with a naive Bayes activity classifier accurately maps SVN log events to activities in real time (average precision/recall/F-measure of about 0.83-0.87 for ArgoUML and 0.68-0.84 for jEdit), outperforming a simpler fuzzy-clustering/path-name-based mapping baseline.
limitations: Authors note the size of the software process log sample is limited, the weighting of certain features used in event mapping lacks a standardized measure, and there is no standard method for evaluating unsupervised clustering results.

limitations: not stated

main_finding: The paper presents an algorithm that automatically translates SGTS models (nodes, edges, rules) into PRISM's continuous-time Markov chain input language, demonstrated on a toy mobile-network case study where safety and liveness properties were specified in CSL and successfully verified via PRISM model checking.
